stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. In the Route 53 public hosted zone, app.example.com is an A record that holds the IP addresses of the load balancer. An engineer copied the addresses when the load balancer was created. The name receives millions of DNS queries each month. Users now report intermittent connection errors, mostly after traffic peaks. The company wants to stop the errors. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?
keywords: holds the IP addresses of the load balancer
millions of DNS queries each month
intermittent connection errors, mostly after traffic peaks

options.text: Replace the A record with a CNAME record for app.example.com whose value is the DNS name that AWS assigned to the Application Load Balancer.
options.why: It works, because the name follows the load balancer, but Route 53 [charges for CNAME queries](../facts/route53.md#route53-alias-queries-free-cname-charged), so it costs more than an alias record.

options.text: Create a scheduled AWS Lambda function that reads the current load balancer addresses every minute and writes them into the A record for app.example.com.
options.why: The function adds cost, and resolvers keep the old addresses [according to their time to live (TTL)](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-resolver-caches-by-ttl-outside-control) after each rewrite.
options.misconception: believes that rewriting the record every minute keeps every user on the current addresses

options.text: Associate Elastic IP addresses with the Application Load Balancer, and replace the values of the A record for app.example.com with those Elastic IP addresses.
options.why: Elastic IP addresses do not attach to an Application Load Balancer: in the feature table, [IP address - Static, Elastic](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-static-elastic-ip-nlb-only) belongs to the [Network Load Balancer](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-static-elastic-ip-nlb-only).

options.text: Replace the A record with an alias record of type A for app.example.com that points to the Application Load Balancer.
options.why: Route 53 follows the address changes of the load balancer for an alias record, and Amazon Route 53 [doesn't charge for alias queries to ELB](../facts/route53.md#route53-alias-elb-no-query-charge) load balancers.

explanation: Elastic Load Balancing scales the load balancer and updates its DNS entry with a [time-to-live (TTL) of 60 seconds](../facts/route53.md#route53-elb-dns-entry-updated-ttl-60), so copied addresses go stale after peaks. With an alias record, [Route 53 detects changes in the resource on its own](../facts/route53.md#route53-alias-follows-resource-ip-changes) and answers with the current addresses. With millions of queries a month, the query charge is what separates a CNAME record from an alias record.
takeaway: Point a name at a load balancer with an alias record: Route 53 follows its changing addresses at no query charge.
twin: If the stem said "app.example.com must point to a host name of a partner outside AWS" instead: a CNAME record, because an alias record [can only redirect queries to selected AWS resources](../facts/route53.md#route53-alias-targets-only-selected-aws-resources).

stem: A company serves www.example.com from three Amazon EC2 instances that have Elastic IP addresses. Route 53 answers with three weighted A records, each with a nonzero weight and its own health check. During a failed deployment, all three instances failed their health checks, but users still received the addresses of the failed instances. When no instance is healthy, users must see a static error page from an S3 bucket named www.example.com that is configured as a website. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: each with a nonzero weight and its own health check
users still received the addresses of the failed instances

options.text: Rename the three weighted records, then create failover records for www.example.com: an alias record for the weighted records as the primary, and the S3 website as the secondary.
options.why: It works with more effort: [You can't create non-failover records](../facts/route53.md#route53-failover-no-non-failover-record-same-name-type) with the name and type of failover records, so the weighted records need new names.

options.text: Lower the TTL of the three weighted records to 60 seconds, so that resolvers drop the failed addresses soon after Route 53 stops returning the unhealthy records.
options.why: When no record is healthy, Route 53 [considers all the records in the group](../facts/route53.md#route53-no-record-healthy-all-records-considered-healthy) healthy and keeps returning them, so no error page appears.

options.text: Add a fourth weighted record for www.example.com: an alias record for the S3 website endpoint with a weight of 0, and keep the three records as they are.
options.why: [All the records with nonzero weights must be unhealthy](../facts/route53.md#route53-failover-weighted-zero-weight-caveat) before Route 53 answers with a record that has a weight of 0, so the S3 website answers only when no instance is healthy.

options.text: Add a weighted alias record for the S3 website endpoint with a weight of 0, and remove the health checks from the three records so that failed instances are left out.
options.why: When a record has no health check, Route 53 [always considers it healthy](../facts/route53.md#route53-record-without-health-check-always-healthy), so the failed instances keep their share of users.

explanation: Route 53 has [a mode of last resort](../facts/route53.md#route53-last-resort-mode-all-unhealthy-returns-answer): when every record is unhealthy, it answers with them anyway, which is why users got the failed addresses. A record with a weight of 0 waits behind the nonzero records, and the bucket already has the [same name as your domain or subdomain](../facts/route53.md#route53-s3-website-bucket-name-must-match).
takeaway: A weighted record with a weight of 0 answers when every nonzero weighted record is unhealthy.
twin: If the stem said "each weighted record has no health check" instead: first add a health check to each record, because Route 53 [always considers it healthy](../facts/route53.md#route53-record-without-health-check-always-healthy) when a record has none.

stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer in us-east-1. A copy of the application runs the same way in us-west-2. A failed instance must be replaced automatically. When the whole application in us-east-1 fails, users must be sent to us-west-2. Which solution will provide a highly available design with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: A failed instance must be replaced automatically
When the whole application in us-east-1 fails

options.text: Create a Route 53 health check for each instance, so that Route 53 replaces a failed instance and sends users to us-west-2 when every check fails.
options.why: A Route 53 health check changes DNS answers: [Route 53 routes traffic away from the associated record](../facts/route53.md#route53-dns-failover-routes-traffic-away-from-unhealthy-record), but nothing in Route 53 replaces an instance.

options.text: Turn on ELB health checks for both Auto Scaling groups, so that the us-east-1 load balancer sends users to us-west-2 when all of its targets fail.
options.why: A load balancer acts on its own targets: [it stops routing traffic to that target](../facts/elb.md#elb-unhealthy-target-stop-resume), and the DNS answer that sends users to us-east-1 stays the same.
options.misconception: believes that a load balancer sends users to another Region when all of its targets fail

options.text: Turn on ELB health checks for both Auto Scaling groups, and run a scheduled script that points the record to us-west-2 when the us-east-1 load balancer fails.
options.why: It works, but the team writes, runs and tests the script, and failover records with Evaluate Target Health switch without any code.

options.text: Turn on ELB health checks for both Auto Scaling groups, and create failover alias records for the two load balancers with Evaluate Target Health on the primary.
options.why: With ELB health checks, [Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling replaces the unhealthy instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-checks-reroute-and-replace), and the failover records answer with us-west-2 when the primary load balancer is unhealthy.

explanation: Each health check changes a different thing. With ELB health checks on the group, [Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling replaces the unhealthy instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-checks-reroute-and-replace). For the Region, DNS failover for an ELB endpoint uses an alias record with the [“Evaluate Target Health” parameter to true](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-elb-failover-alias-evaluate-target-health), so Route 53 can [route traffic away from unhealthy resources](../facts/route53.md#route53-evaluate-target-health-benefit-for-elb-beanstalk).
takeaway: Auto Scaling replaces instances, a load balancer avoids failed targets, and Route 53 moves users between Regions.
twin: If the stem said "both Regions must serve users at the same time" instead: latency or weighted alias records with Evaluate Target Health, because Route 53 then answers [a DNS query using any healthy record](../facts/route53.md#route53-active-active-failover-definition).
